cherry-heering: Cherry Heering has been made since 1818, when Peter Frederik Suhm Heering, a young Copenhagen merchant, began producing a liqueur of Danish cherries steeped in spirit with spices. His firm grew into a trading house that carried the liqueur well beyond Denmark, and it became a purveyor to the Royal Danish Court. It found its lasting place in cocktails such as the Singapore Sling and the Blood and Sand.
gammel-dansk: Gammel Dansk went on sale in 1967 after three years of development at Danish Distillers in Roskilde, where the factory manager and master blender J. K. Asmund worked out its blend of twenty-nine herbs, spices and flowers. The name means old Danish, suggesting a tradition far older than the recipe. In 2014 its owner, Arcus, announced that production would move to Norway.
brannvin: Brännvin, burnt wine, is the old Nordic word for distilled spirit, and its earliest Swedish mentions, from the fifteenth century, concern its use in making gunpowder rather than drinking. Distilling from grain and later potatoes spread through Swedish farms until the state restricted home distilling and finally banned it in the mid-nineteenth century. In the late nineteenth century Lars Olsson Smith sold a purer, rectified brännvin, the forerunner of Absolut.
swedish-punsch: Swedish punsch began with Batavia arrack from Java, which the Swedish East India Company started bringing home to Gothenburg in the 1730s. Punch made with it quickly became fashionable among those who could afford imported spirit, sugar and tea, and in the mid-nineteenth century Johan Cederlund's firm became the first to sell it ready-made in bottles. Student societies wrote songs in its honour, and it is still served warm with the Thursday supper of pea soup and pancakes.
baska-droppar: Bäska droppar, bitter drops, is a Swedish brännvin flavoured with wormwood, part of the country's long tradition of bitter herbal snaps.
linie-aquavit: The Linie story begins in 1805, when a ship sailed from Trondheim to the East Indies with casks of aquavit among its cargo and returned two years later. The story goes that aquavit that had made the round trip came back tasting better for the rolling sea and the swings of temperature. The Lysholm distillery in Trondheim later made the voyage a deliberate practice, and Linie is still shipped across the equator, the line that gives it its name, before it is bottled.
lakka: Lakka is the Finnish word for cloudberry, and this amber liqueur is made from the wild berries of the bogs and fells of northern Finland.
mesimarja: Mesimarja is the Finnish name for the arctic bramble, Rubus arcticus, a sparsely fruiting northern berry that gives this Finnish liqueur its name and its perfume.
jaloviina: Alko, the Finnish state alcohol company, began making Jaloviina in 1932, after the country's prohibition ended, as a cut brandy: brandy blended with grain spirit. It was modelled on a blended brandy then popular in Sweden, and it has stayed in production ever since. The stars on the label show how much brandy is in the blend, Finns nickname the grades after military ranks, from vänrikki to kapteeni, and the whole range is known as Jallu.
salmiakki-koskenkorva: Koskenkorva takes its name from the village in Ilmajoki, western Finland, where its barley spirit is distilled. Homemade salmiakki spirit, made by dissolving salty liquorice sweets in Koskenkorva, was already popular when Alko, the state alcohol company, put a bottled Salmiakki Koskenkorva on sale for the New Year of 1993. Known as salmari or salmiakkikossu, it owes its bite to ammonium chloride, the salt that gives salmiakki its name.
brennivin: Brennivín was first produced in 1935, when Iceland partially lifted its prohibition and the newly founded State Alcohol Company began making a spirit flavoured only with caraway. The government demanded a stark black label to warn against consumption, which earned the drink the nickname svarti dauði, black death. The design was meant to limit demand and instead became the brand's signature.
zubrowka: Bison grass vodka is traced to the sixteenth century, when Polish distillers are said to have begun flavouring spirit with a grass from the Białowieża Forest, known as bison grass after the żubr, the European bison that lives there. Commercial production began in 1928, and the brand is still made at Polmos Białystok. Because the grass contains coumarin, the United States long kept it off shelves, and since 2011 a reformulated version has been sold there.
starka: Starka, from the Polish stary, old, is rye spirit matured in oak, a tradition of the old Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. As the custom is told, a father would fill a barrel at a child's birth, seal it and bury it, and open it at the child's wedding. Traditional recipes add linden and apple leaves during ageing, and the Szczecin distillery that carries the Starka name is now its main Polish producer.
krupnik: Krupnik is a spiced honey liqueur of Poland and Lithuania, where it is called krupnikas, and it is usually traced to the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth of the sixteenth century or earlier.
nalewka: Nalewka, from the Polish nalewać, to pour, is the Polish household tradition of steeping fruit, herbs, roots or nuts in spirit, sweetening them and leaving them to mature.
spirytus-rektyfikowany: Spirytus rektyfikowany is Polish rectified spirit, sold at about 95 percent and bought mainly as an ingredient for nalewki, fruit liqueurs and preserves.
becherovka: Becherovka began in 1807, when Josef Vitus Becher, a Carlsbad merchant, started selling a herbal bitter he had spent two years testing from a recipe worked out with Christian Frobrig, a visiting physician. It was first sold as English Bitter, and Becher's son Johann Nepomuk built the business into a factory from 1838. After the Second World War the drink took the name Becherovka, and the company says only two people know the full recipe and may enter the room where the herbs are mixed.
fernet-stock: Fernet Stock has been made at Božkov, near Plzeň, since 1927, by the company Lionello Stock had founded in Trieste with Carlo Camis in 1884 and extended into Czechoslovakia after the First World War. The Italian-style bitter took root so thoroughly that most Czechs think of it as their own. A citrus version followed in 1997 and quickly became one of the country's most popular spirits.
tuzemak: Tuzemák grew out of the Habsburg empire's taste for rum and its lack of cane-growing colonies: distillers in Bohemia and Moravia made a domestic substitute from sugar-beet spirit flavoured with rum essence and sold it as tuzemský rum, domestic rum. When the Czech Republic joined the European Union, rules reserving the word rum for cane spirit forced a new name, and producers settled on tuzemák. Many Czechs still simply call it rum.
hruskovice: Hruškovice, from hruška, pear, is the pear brandy of the Czech and Slovak fruit-distilling tradition, most often made from Williams pears.
merunkovice: Meruňkovice is the apricot brandy of South Moravia's orchards, a cousin of Austria's Marillenbrand and Hungary's barackpálinka.
czech-absinth: Czech absinth as it is sold today dates from the early 1990s, when Radomil Hill, whose family liqueur firm had been founded by Albín Hill in 1920, began producing it. Exports of Hill's to Britain later that decade helped spark a wider absinthe revival, though claims that the firm made absinth before the war remain unproven. Many Czech versions contain little or no anise, so they do not cloud with water, and the ritual of setting fire to a sugar cube is credited to Czech drinkers of the 1990s rather than to the French tradition.
borovicka: Borovička takes its name from borievka, the Slovak word for juniper, and is Slovakia's juniper spirit, several regional versions of which carry EU geographical indications.
demanovka: Demänovka is a Slovak herbal liqueur named after the Demänová valley in the Low Tatras, near Liptovský Mikuláš, and made in sweet and bitter versions.
torkolypalinka: Törkölypálinka is the pomace branch of Hungary's pálinka tradition, distilled from the grape skins and seeds left after winemaking and protected under the same Hungarian rules as fruit pálinka.
unicum: Unicum is traced to 1790, when Dr József Zwack, physician to the Habsburg court, is said to have created the bitter for Emperor Joseph II, who supposedly declared it ein Unikum, a unique thing. The Zwack family built a distillery in Pest, but after the communist takeover the business was nationalised and the family went into exile, while the state produced its own version. After the fall of communism Péter Zwack returned and restored production to the original recipe.
zganje: Žganje, from the Slovene žgati, to burn, is Slovenia's household fruit brandy, distilled from plums, pears, apples or whatever the orchard yields.
brinjevec: Brinjevec takes its name from brin, the Slovene word for juniper, and is made by fermenting and distilling the berries themselves, which makes it closer to a fruit brandy than to gin.
pelinkovec: Pelinkovec takes its name from pelin, the South Slavic word for wormwood, and is the dark wormwood bitter of Slovenia, Croatia and their neighbours.
samogon: Samogon, self-distilled, is the home-made spirit of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus, distilled from grain, sugar beet, potatoes or fruit.
nastoyka: Nastoyka, from the Russian word for infusion, is vodka steeped with fruit, berries, roots, herbs or spices, a tradition kept in Russian homes and by commercial distillers alike.
horilka: Horilka, from the Ukrainian hority, to burn, is Ukraine's word for strong spirit and its own vodka tradition, often flavoured with honey, pepper, herbs or fruit.
pertsivka: Pertsivka, from perets, pepper, is Ukrainian horilka infused with chilli peppers and often honey, frequently bottled with whole chillies inside.
krambambulya: The name Krambambuli first belonged to a red cherry liqueur from a distillery in Danzig, now Gdańsk, and it travelled widely through a German student song. In Belarus it names something different, spirit warmed with honey and spices, which Belarusian tradition links to the gentry of the old Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and producers there now bottle it as a liqueur.
riga-black-balsam: Riga Black Balsam is traced to 1752, when Abraham Kunze, an apothecary in Riga, created a herbal balsam whose recipe is still the basis of the drink. It is now made by Latvijas Balzams from twenty-four ingredients and sold in a dark ceramic bottle, and the company says only its head liquor master and two apprentices know the exact recipe.
trejos-devynerios: Trejos devynerios, three nines, is a Lithuanian herbal bitter named for the twenty-seven herbs, roots and spices in its blend.
vana-tallinn: Vana Tallinn, Old Tallinn, was created in 1960 at the Tallinn distillery now called Liviko, its recipe devised by master distiller Ilse Maar with Bernhard Jürno and Jaan Siimo. The rum-based blend with citrus, vanilla and cinnamon became the classic souvenir of Soviet-era Tallinn and has been made without interruption since. It remained a single product until variants at other strengths appeared in 1999, and it is now sold in dozens of countries.
orujo: Orujo is the pomace spirit of Galicia, distilled from the skins and seeds left after winemaking, and the base of the queimada, a flamed punch served while a spell called the conxuro is recited.
pacharan: Pacharán takes its name from patxaran, the Basque word for sloe, and is Navarre's liqueur of wild sloes steeped in anise spirit, now protected as Pacharán Navarro.
licor-43: Licor 43 was launched in 1946 in Cartagena by the Zamora siblings and their partner Emilio Restoy, who named it for the forty-three ingredients in its recipe. The company links it to a legendary golden elixir of ancient Carthago Nova, the city's Roman name, a story that cannot be verified. The family firm, Diego Zamora, has since made it one of the most widely distributed Spanish liqueurs.
anis: Anise spirits have been distilled in Spain for centuries, with towns such as Chinchón and Cazalla known for them, but one of the best-known bottles came from Badalona in the second half of the nineteenth century. There the brothers Vicente and José Bosch launched Anís del Mono, whose monkey label is often read as a joke about Darwin, though other explanations exist. A poster competition the firm held at the end of the century produced Ramon Casas's celebrated design.
hierbas: Hierbas is the herbal anise liqueur of the Balearic Islands, made by steeping local plants such as rosemary, fennel and thyme in anise spirit and protected as Hierbas de Mallorca and Hierbas Ibicencas.
ron-miel: Ron miel is Canary Islands rum blended with honey, a regional style from islands that have grown sugarcane since the fifteenth century, now protected as Ronmiel de Canarias.
aguardente-vinica: Aguardente vínica is Portuguese wine brandy, best known as the grape spirit added to port to stop its fermentation, and Lourinhã, north of Lisbon, is a region demarcated for brandy alone.
aguardente-bagaceira: Bagaceira takes its name from bagaço, Portuguese for grape pomace, and is the pomace brandy of Portugal's wine regions, above all the north.
medronho: Medronho is distilled from the fruit of the strawberry tree, Arbutus unedo, which grows wild in the hills of the Algarve and Alentejo, especially around Monchique.
ginjinha: Lisbon credits ginjinha, from ginja, the sour cherry, to Francisco Espinheira, a Galician who steeped the cherries in aguardente with sugar and cinnamon, though accounts differ on whether he was himself a friar or took a friar's advice. The bar at Largo de São Domingos that carries his name dates its beginnings to 1840 and still pours it. In Óbidos it is often served in a small cup of dark chocolate, eaten once the drink is finished.
licor-beirao: Licor Beirão began in the nineteenth century as a pharmacy preparation in Lousã, in the Beira region, and went on being made in a small factory run by the original maker's son-in-law. It took its name in 1929, when it won a gold medal at the second Beirão Congress in Castelo Branco. In 1940 José Carranca Redondo bought the factory and the secret recipe, and his advertising, proclaiming it the liqueur of Portugal, made it a national brand.
aguardente-de-cana: Aguardente de cana is Madeira's cane spirit, distilled from fresh sugarcane juice rather than molasses, protected as Rum da Madeira and best known as the base of poncha.
italian-brandy: Italian brandy grew into an industry in the nineteenth century, and one of its founding houses was set up in Bologna by Jean Bouton, a French distiller who italianised his name to Buton. Italian producers long sold their brandy as cognac, until international rules reserved that name for France, which is how Cognac Buton became Vecchia Romagna. Gabriele d'Annunzio is credited with coining arzente as an Italian alternative, but brandy is the word that stuck.
amaro: Amaro, Italian for bitter, covers a family of herbal liqueurs that grew from monastery and pharmacy preparations. Many of the famous names date from the nineteenth century, when men such as Ausano Ramazzotti, a pharmacist in Milan, and Salvatore Averna in Caltanissetta turned recipes into brands. Nearly every region has its own, using local herbs, roots and citrus, and no single first amaro can be named.
mirto: Mirto is Sardinia's myrtle liqueur, the red made from the ripe dark berries and the white from the young leaves and shoots of the shrub that grows wild across the island.
strega: Strega was created in 1860 in Benevento by Giuseppe Alberti, whose family business turned a recipe of some seventy herbs and spices, coloured gold with saffron, into a brand. The name means witch, after Benevento's old legends of witches gathering under a walnut tree, and the branding has embraced it ever since. In 1947 Guido Alberti, with the writer Maria Bellonci, founded the Premio Strega, now one of Italy's most important literary prizes.
galliano: Galliano was created in 1896 in Livorno by the distiller Arturo Vaccari, who named it after Giuseppe Galliano, an Italian officer who had become famous for defending a fort at Mekele during the First Italo-Ethiopian War. Its vanilla and anise recipe and tall bottle, shaped like a classical Roman column, made it stand out on back bars. It gained international fame in the seventies through the Harvey Wallbanger, a vodka and orange drink topped with a float of Galliano.
frangelico: Frangelico was launched in 1978 in Canale, in Piedmont, a region known for its Tonda Gentile hazelnuts. Its name draws on a legend, promoted by the makers, of a hermit monk called Fra Angelico who lived in the Piedmont hills and devised liqueur recipes, and the bottle imitates a friar's habit, complete with a cord at the waist. The brand has passed through several owners and has belonged to Campari since 2010.
tsipouro: Tsipouro, the pomace spirit of mainland Greece, is traditionally credited to Orthodox monks on Mount Athos in the fourteenth century. It became the farm spirit of Thessaly, Epirus and Macedonia, where families distil after the grape harvest, with or without anise depending on the region. Regional names, including tsipouro of Tyrnavos, are protected under EU rules.
tsikoudia: Tsikoudia takes its name from tsikouda, the Cretan word for the pomace left after pressing grapes, and is Crete's unflavoured pomace spirit, protected as a geographical indication.
mastiha: Mastiha is a liqueur flavoured with mastic, the resin of trees that yield it in quantity only in the southern villages of Chios, where the know-how of cultivating it is recognised by UNESCO.
metaxa: Metaxa was created in 1888 by Spyros Metaxas, a merchant from a silk-trading family, who blended aged wine distillate with muscat wine and a botanical infusion, producing a spirit that sits outside the usual definition of brandy. Its emblem, the Salamis warrior, was inspired by an ancient medallion reportedly found while his distillery in Piraeus was being built. The stars on the label indicate the age and grade of the blend.
kumquat-liqueur: Kumquat liqueur is a speciality of Corfu, where the kumquat tree is credited to Sidney Merlin, a British botanist who lived on the island, and where the fruit is also made into preserves and sweets.
zivania: Zivania's origins are unclear: some trace it to the end of the fifteenth century, when Venice ruled Cyprus, and others credit monks from Mount Athos with bringing the method. It is distilled from grape pomace mixed with local dry wine made from Xynisteri and Mavro grapes, and its name is protected under EU rules for Cyprus alone.
filfar: Filfar is a Cypriot orange liqueur, and its makers trace the recipe to an old Venetian manuscript found on the island, a claim that cannot be checked.
bajtra: Bajtra is the Maltese word for prickly pear, the cactus fruit from the Americas that grows along the islands' rubble walls, and the liqueur is a modern product made from its ripe fruit.
rakija: Rakija, the fruit brandy of the Balkans, takes its name from the Arabic araq by way of the Turkish rakı, and distilling it is generally thought to have spread across the peninsula during the Ottoman centuries. Every country and region has its fruit: plum in Serbia and Bosnia, grapes along the Adriatic, apricots, pears and quinces in the orchards in between. The Serbian tradition of making šljivovica, plum rakija, is inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
travarica: Travarica, from trava, herb or grass, is grape rakija infused with wild herbs, the traditional welcome drink of the Dalmatian coast and its hinterland.
biska: Biska is an Istrian mistletoe rakija closely associated with Hum, the tiny hilltop town in central Istria, and local tradition attributes the recipe to the Celtic Druids, though nobody has managed to date it.
lozovaca: Lozovača, from loza, the vine, is grape rakija made from pomace or whole grapes, the spirit of the wine-growing coast and hills of Croatia, Serbia and Montenegro.
kajsijevaca: Kajsijevača, from kajsija, apricot, is apricot rakija, one of the fruit brandies of Serbia's household distilling tradition.
dunjevaca: Dunjevača, from dunja, quince, is quince rakija, one of the most prized of Serbia's fruit brandies.
medovaca: Medovača, from med, honey, is rakija sweetened with honey and often infused with herbs, made across Serbia and the western Balkans on a plum or grape base.
kruskovaca: Kruškovača, from kruška, pear, is pear rakija from Bosnia and its neighbours, usually made from the Williams pear.
loza: Loza, the vine, is Montenegro's grape rakija, distilled after the harvest along the coast and in the vineyards around Lake Skadar.
mastika: Mastika is an anise spirit of North Macedonia and Bulgaria, named after mastic resin, and despite the shared name it is a different drink from the mastiha liqueur of Chios.
menta: Menta is Bulgaria's bright green peppermint liqueur, made by steeping mint in spirit and often mixed with mastika.
tuica: Țuică is Romania's plum spirit, distilled once from fermented plums in the villages of the Carpathian foothills and Transylvania.
palinca: Palincă is the double-distilled fruit spirit of Transylvania, stronger than the once-distilled țuică, and it shares its name and much of its history with Hungarian pálinka.
visinata: Vișinată, from vișină, sour cherry, is a Romanian household liqueur made by steeping sour cherries with sugar in spirit through the summer.
afinata: Afinată, from afină, bilberry, is a Romanian liqueur made by steeping wild bilberries from the Carpathian forests in spirit with sugar.
skanderbeg: Skanderbeg is an Albanian grape brandy named after Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg, the fifteenth-century lord who led Albanian resistance to the Ottoman Empire and remains the national hero.
chacha: Chacha is the pomace brandy of Georgia, distilled from the grape skins and stems left after winemaking in a country with one of the world's oldest wine traditions.
armenian-brandy: Armenian brandy began in 1887, when the merchant Nerses Tairyants opened a wine and brandy factory in Yerevan. In 1899 he sold it to the Russian industrialist Nikolai Shustov, whose brandies won fame across the Russian Empire, and the Yerevan Brandy Company now makes the Ararat range. A popular story holds that Winston Churchill was sent cases of it by Stalin after tasting it at Yalta, but it rests on anecdote rather than documents.
oghi: Oghi is the Armenian word for fruit spirit, distilled in villages across the country from mulberries, cornelian cherries, apricots, grapes and other fruit.
tutovka: Tutovka, from tut, the word for mulberry across much of the Caucasus and Central Asia, is spirit distilled from fermented mulberries in Azerbaijan and the surrounding mountains.
southern-comfort: Southern Comfort was created in 1874 by Martin Wilkes Heron, a bartender at McCauley's Tavern in New Orleans, who blended whiskey with fruit and spices to improve the rough spirit of the day. He first called it Cuffs and Buttons before settling on its present name, and after moving to Memphis he bottled it under the slogan none genuine but mine. For decades the recipe used neutral spirit as its base, and whiskey returned to it after Sazerac bought the brand in 2016.
okolehao: Ōkolehao is credited to William Stevenson, an escaped British convict who reached Hawaii in the 1790s and began distilling the fermented, baked root of the ti plant. The name means iron bottom, after the iron try pots from sailing ships that served as stills. It found new popularity in Hawaii during the Second World War, when grain spirits were rationed, and faded as imported spirits returned.
canadian-rye: Canada's whisky industry took shape in the nineteenth century, when millers such as Gooderham and Worts in Toronto and Hiram Walker in Windsor began distilling their grain. Adding rye to a largely wheat or corn mash gave the whisky its spice, and rye became the popular name for Canadian whisky whatever the recipe. Canadian rules allow a small share of other spirits or wine in the blend, and some distillers now make it from mashes of rye alone.
screech: Screech grew from Newfoundland's salt cod trade with Jamaica, which sent rum north in exchange for fish. When the Newfoundland government took control of liquor sales in the twentieth century it began bottling the rum under its own label, and a popular story says the name came from an American serviceman's reaction to his first taste during the Second World War, though screech was already slang for rough spirit. The screech-in, a mock ceremony for visitors involving a cod and a recitation, keeps it central to island hospitality.
maple-liqueur: Maple liqueur is a modern Quebec product, blending Canadian whisky or neutral spirit with maple syrup from the province that makes most of the world's supply.
charanda: Charanda comes from the country around Uruapan in Michoacán, where sugarcane was planted after the Spanish conquest, and it takes its name from the Cerro de la Charanda, a hill near the city where the region's first distillery is said to have stood. In Purépecha the word means red-coloured earth. Early in the twenty-first century charanda received a Mexican denomination of origin, and it is rarely seen outside Mexico.
comiteco: Comiteco takes its name from Comitán de Domínguez in Chiapas, where distilling is said to have arrived with Dominican friars in the colonial period, and it is made from aguamiel, the sweet sap tapped from living agaves, rather than from roasted agave hearts. Tax changes and a shortage of agave nearly ended commercial production in the twentieth century, leaving only artisanal makers. Producers around Comitán have since revived it, and it remains rare outside Chiapas.
kahlua: Kahlúa was first produced in Veracruz in 1936, blending local arabica coffee with sugarcane spirit, with Pedro Domecq behind its production. The name is usually explained as Veracruz Nahuatl for house of the Acolhua people. Jules Berman, who first imported it into the United States, became known as Mr Kahlúa, and its American success made it a staple of mixed drinks such as the Black Russian and the White Russian.
rompope: Rompope is traditionally credited to the nuns of the Santa Clara convent in Puebla, who are said to have made it in the seventeenth century with rum or cane spirit, milk, sugar, egg yolks and cinnamon. Its name is usually linked to rompón, a Spanish eggnog that reached Mexico. It is now bottled commercially across the country and is a fixture of Mexican Christmas celebrations.
xtabentun: Xtabentún takes its name from the Maya word for a morning glory that blooms across Yucatán and whose nectar feeds local bees. Long before the Spanish arrived, the Maya made balché, a ceremonial fermented drink of honey and tree bark, and the modern liqueur is usually seen as its descendant, with anise and distillation brought by Europeans. Distilleries in Yucatán still make it from honey, anise and rum.
damiana: Damiana is a Mexican herbal liqueur made from the leaves of Turnera diffusa, a shrub native to Baja California and other parts of Mexico.
guatemalan-rum: Guatemala's modern rum industry is closely tied to the Botrán family, five brothers from Burgos in Spain who founded Industria Licorera Quezalteca in 1939, the start of what became Industrias Licoreras de Guatemala. In 1976 the company created Ron Zacapa to mark the centenary of the town of Zacapa, distilling from virgin sugarcane honey, a concentrated cane juice, rather than molasses. Its rums, aged in the highlands of Quetzaltenango, gave Guatemalan rum an international reputation.
quetzalteca: Quetzalteca takes its name from Quetzaltenango, in Guatemala's western highlands, and is the country's everyday clear cane aguardiente, sold plain and in fruit flavours.
honduran-aguardiente: Honduran aguardiente is a clear cane spirit, often with a light anise note, and its best-known name, Yuscarán, comes from a colonial silver-mining town in the department of El Paraíso.
cususa: Cususa is the unlicensed cane spirit of Nicaragua's northern highlands, distilled in improvised stills and sold without labels.
guaro: Guaro, short for aguardiente, is Costa Rica's cane spirit, and its production has been controlled by the state since the mid-nineteenth century, when the government nationalised it and set up a national liquor factory to stamp out illegal distilling. The Fábrica Nacional de Licores still makes Cacique, the dominant brand, as a light, near-neutral spirit designed to mix. Guaro remains the base of the country's simple mixed drinks, from the guaro sour to the chiliguaro.
seco-herrerano: Seco Herrerano comes from Pesé, in Panama's Herrera province, where the Varela family business dates its beginnings to 1908. The family's company, Varela Hermanos, distils local sugarcane three times into a clean, light spirit that took the province's name and became Panama's national drink, while the same firm later built a reputation abroad with aged rums. A popular local serve, seco con leche, mixes it with milk over ice.
